title: Friars hours, Valentino Inn, and auditioning for Ted Lewis
summary: After Friars he leads at the Valentino Inn, wins a Ted Lewis audition at the Apollo, dresses up for Broadway, and gets news of his mother's death.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Well, we went to work at, uh, well, we'd switched. First we went to work early, then we'd switch and went to work late. We'd get in there about, uh, ten o'clock. We'd be, we'd first, we'd went from eight until, uh, two. Then it changed the hours. The business picked up so good that we started going into ten and going through four and five in the morning. That's when we used to get good overtime. We made good money there. So then, that band broke up after so long, of time, and then, uh, I get the job at the Valentino Inn, which was on Adams Street, was owned by Dan Barone. And then, uh, I had Kyle Pierce on piano, Caffarelli on, uh, Gene Caffarelli on trumpet, Bill Paley on drums, uh, Dale Skinner on saxophone, and I sent to New Orleans for Chink Martin on bass. And, uh, we stayed there. We played up in the balcony, and we stayed there a while. And they used to do a couple of shootings in there, federal men shooting, uh, uh, bootleggers. So then, one night, Ted Lewis walked in. He says, boy, he says, I want you for my band. I says, well, Mr. Lewis, I says, I'm working here. I'm a leader. He says, well, he says, come down and have an audition for me. So he was at the Apollo Theater now, which is known as the, uh, uh, It's the United Artists now, isn't it? Maybe, I'm not sure. Yeah, that's now known as the United Artists' Theater. And it was with a thing called the, uh, 1923 Passing Show. So I go down there, and there's about 25 trombone players sitting there. So the tune called, uh, Dreamy Melody was popular then, and, uh, me, I was playing the Tiger X 40 times a night. So he asked me to audition. I played a solo, Pretty Melody, uh, Dreamy Melody, and he liked it. And we played the St. Louis Blues, not his arrangement, but, and we played Tiger X. So he come over, he says, listen, bub, he says, the job is yours. He says, but I have to show courtesy to these other boys. He says, I have to listen to them. He says, but the contract is yours. So I went out, and that's when my, at that time my brother Henry, who was to me the world's greatest trombone player, God bless him. And my brother Merritt, when we left the Fry's Inn, I called my brother Merritt and tried to get Chris Mann's band from the Plantation Hollywood, and they had a big band. So Mike heard the band over the phone, he liked it, and then Chris Mann didn't like Chicago, so my brother took the band over Merritt. And Merritt and Henry had the band. So after I went back and told them the news that I got the job at Lewis, I was broke as usual, and, uh, I said, look, I need some money. I said, man, these guys must be sharp guys on Broadway. They walked down the street, they said, here goes Ted Lewis's band. I went out and brought a, brought a derby hat and a beautiful brown top coat and pair of shoes and spats and everything. I want to look like a Broadway guy. So when I walked in there, I go back to the dressing room, I said, man, this is that famous Ted Lewis band. Look at this room, look how these guys live. So that all went by. So the first day I get on the stage with Ted, I've never been on the stage before and I was nervous. And all the girls were, the chorus girls were feeding me mint, you know, to keep my mouth wet. So Ted gets a wire. My mother died in the war. So, uh, I was broke. So Ted knew it all through the show and he let me finish the show. So after the show, he says, son, he says, I got some bad news for you. He says, uh, your mother passed away. So I go into it and he says, what are you going to do? He says, you want to go home? I says, well, I'm kind of short on a little money. I'm still losing. He's peel out $200. He says, here, this will get you home. He says, if you want to come back, he says, let me know. So my brother, brothers and I, we got together and went down for the funeral. And then after my mother, they buried my mother, I came back up and I've been, I've stayed with him for 17 years, off and on, you know. Yeah. Yeah. So then we traveled here, we traveled to Europe, we traveled all over. We had Jimmy Dorsey one time and Don Murray, who was a great saxophone. Both of them were great. And, uh, we made some records with, uh, Benny Goodman, Fats Wara, some of the finest records Lewis made.
